anyway adverb

to move on, or to come back to the point

also but enough of that, so much for that, to get back to the point, but I digress, enough of this!

classical

Cic. Fam. 9.24.1–2: sed haec hāctenus. tē ad cēnās itāre dēsīsse molestē ferō
Cic. Att. 16.7.6: sed haec hāctenus; reliqua cōram

1hāctenus: long a (Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked). The ablative hāc with tenus, which Vergil still writes apart (hāc Trōjāna tenus, Verg. A. 6.62); Lewis & Short marks the same long vowel in quātenus and eātenus.

sed haec hāctenus1

phrase: hāctenus, so far and no further

but enough of that; anyway

Cicero’s way of closing one subject and turning to the next, very frequent in his letters (Lewis & Short: “so much for this”).

Other words

  • sed ut ad rem redeam — but to get back to the point

    also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 7.13.2: sed ut ad rem redeam, tē istīc invītum nōn esse vehementer gaudeō; Cic. Fam. 3.7.6

    After a digression. Shorter, sed ad rem redeō (Cic. Att. 5.21.13) or redeāmus ad nostrum (Cic. Att. 7.11.3).

Examples

  • sed haec hāctenus. tē ad cēnās itāre dēsīsse molestē ferō

    but enough of that. I’m sorry you’ve stopped going out to dinnerCic. Fam. 9.24.1–2

  • sed haec hāctenus; reliqua cōram.

    but enough of that; the rest when we meet.Cic. Att. 16.7.6

  • sed ut ad rem redeam, tē istīc invītum nōn esse vehementer gaudeō

    but to get back to the point, I’m very glad you don’t mind being out thereCic. Fam. 7.13.2

  • Haec quidem hāctenus.

    Enough of this!Traupman 97

  • eātenus

    so much for thatTraupman 382

See also anyway, however.
